facts.claim: "Waiting Around to Die" is a cover of a Townes Van Zandt song. The Bandcamp credits list Van Zandt as the writer, published by Bug Music / Silver Dollar Music.
Jim James of My Morning Jacket appears on the Quiet Life EP on this cover.
Jim James plays bass guitar on Quiet Life's version, according to the video description.
The track is credited as 'Waiting Around to Die (with Jim James)' and runs 4:44. Jim James appears courtesy of ATO Records.
'Housebroken Man' and 'Waiting Around To Die' were recorded by Adam Selzer at Type Foundry in Portland, OR.
Mama Bird's SoundCloud page for the title track says it was mixed by Greg Giorgio at Tarquin Studios in Bridgeport, CT. That page covers the EP's title track, not this song specifically.
The Housebroken Man EP came out August 12, 2014 on Mama Bird Recording. It was recorded at five studios, in Portland, New England, South Carolina, Toronto and Nashville.
Frontman Sean W. Spellman said the EP's songs were written when a lot of things were in flux, at weird or rough times in certain relationships.
A review says the EP closes with the Townes Van Zandt cover, with an assist from Jim James. The review's reading is that Quiet Life can turn gut checks to gold despite the EP's worries.

Quiet Life were born in New London, CT and are based in Portland, OR. AllMusic describes them as Pacific Northwest Americana in the vein of the Lumineers, Head and the Heart, Shovels & Rope and Trampled by Turtles. Their discography includes Act Natural (2007), Big Green (2011), Wild Pack (2013) and Foggy (2016).

research.lineage: Quiet Life is a roots-rock and Americana band that moved from Connecticut to Portland, Oregon. Here it covers a classic by the Texas songwriter Townes Van Zandt, with a guest from My Morning Jacket.

draft:
The cruelest line in **Waiting Around to Die** isn't about death. It sits in the second verse, tossed off in a list of relatives: "He beat her with a belt once 'cause she cried." The mother heads to Tennessee, asks the father to take care of the kid, and the song moves on without a pause. That's the method of this Townes Van Zandt song. Terrible things get one line each, and the narrator keeps walking.

Quiet Life, the Americana band born in New London, Connecticut and settled in Portland, Oregon, close their Housebroken Man EP with it. Adam Selzer recorded it at Type Foundry in Portland, and the band doesn't try to roughen it up. An acoustic guitar fingerpicks a steady arpeggio. The drums keep a slow, simple beat with brushes on the snare. The walking bass line comes from Jim James of My Morning Jacket. The recording is dry and clean, the voice set close, high and a little breathy. It sways. Nothing in the band flinches at what the words are saying, and that calm is what lets the words land.

The refrain carries the song. "It's easier than just a-waitin' 'round to die" is the narrator's excuse for everything: the gambling and the booze, the girl in a Tuscaloosa bar who cleaned him out, the wine and the train, the robbery that ends with a posse dragging him back to Muskogee. Each verse is another escape, defended the same way. There's a drifter's pride in that line, a shrug, and under it someone who has never had a reason to stay anywhere. By the prison verse the refrain stops being a choice. The waiting is just two long years of it.

Then the last verse turns the whole song. Out of prison, he finally has a friend who doesn't steal or cheat or drink or lie. "His name's Codeine, he's the nicest thing I've seen." It plays like a joke, and it's the saddest thing in the song, because his idea of kindness is built from everyone who failed him. He's done running. The plan now is to wait.

Frontman Sean W. Spellman has said the EP's songs came from a time when a lot was in flux, with rough stretches in certain relationships. Quiet Life play this borrowed song gently, and that's the right call. The softness keeps you sitting next to the man instead of looking down at him.

It sticks because a man describes his whole ruined life in the same soft, swaying voice he'd use to introduce a friend, and by the end you realize that's exactly what he's doing.
